I am planning dinner for six people this Saturday. Two of them do not eat meat and one cannot have dairy. I want one main dish that everyone can share, plus a couple of sides. I have a large oven, two pans and a slow cooker. I would like to do most of the cooking on Friday evening so that I can spend time with my guests instead of standing at the stove the whole night.

Each week I buy a big bag of spinach, a bunch of carrots, some onions, a block of cheese and a loaf of bread. By Thursday half of the spinach has gone limp and I end up throwing it out. I cook for myself and my partner, and we both work long days. I want a simple routine for the week that uses what I buy before it spoils and does not take more than half an hour each night.

My grandmother used to make a stew with beans, smoked paprika, potatoes and a little bit of sausage. She never wrote anything down. I remember it was thick, a bit smoky and slightly sweet, and she served it with crusty bread. I have tried to make it twice and it came out thin and plain both times. I would like to work out a version that comes close to what I remember from her kitchen.

I started baking sourdough a month ago. My starter bubbles and rises within six hours of feeding. The loaves have a fine flavour but they spread out flat on the tray instead of rising up. I use about seventy percent water, fold the dough four times over two hours and then shape it and leave it in the fridge overnight. My kitchen sits at around twenty degrees most of the day.

We have a small balcony with a few pots of herbs: mint, parsley, thyme and rosemary. The mint is taking over, the parsley looks tired, and the thyme is doing fine. I would like to use more of these in everyday meals instead of letting them grow wild. We mostly cook pasta, rice dishes, eggs and roast vegetables, and we rarely have time for anything fancy during the week.

I am meal prepping lunches for work. At the moment I make one big tray of chicken and rice on Sunday and eat it for five days. By Wednesday I am tired of it. I have a microwave at work but no fridge, so I bring an insulated bag with an ice pack. I would like three or four lunch ideas that keep well, taste different from each other and can be cooked in the same session on a Sunday afternoon.

My son is starting to cook for himself at university. He has a single hob, a small oven and a shared fridge. He likes spicy food, does not like mushrooms and has a budget of about forty pounds a week for food. I would like to give him a short list of dishes he can learn, starting with the simplest and building up, so that he does not live on instant noodles for the whole first term.

I want to get better at making soup without a recipe. I usually start with onions and garlic, add whatever vegetables are in the fridge, pour in stock and let it simmer. It always tastes fine but a little flat. I have heard people talk about balancing salt, acid and fat, and about building flavour in layers. I would like to understand what that means in practice for an ordinary weekday soup.

Next month I am going to Lisbon for five days with two friends. We arrive on a Thursday morning and leave the following Tuesday evening. We like walking, food markets, small museums and sitting by the water. None of us wants to rush from sight to sight. We are staying in an apartment near the centre and would like to take one day trip outside the city, probably by train.

I travel for work about twice a month, usually for two or three nights. I carry a laptop, a change of clothes for each day, a pair of shoes and a small bag of toiletries. I want to fit everything into one small backpack so that I can skip checked bags and the wait at the carousel. I am not sure how to pack shirts so they do not crease, or how to keep the cables tidy.

We are planning a road trip along the coast with two young children, aged four and seven. We will drive about three hours a day and stay in a different place most nights. The kids get restless after an hour in the car. I would like ideas for breaking up the drives, keeping them busy in the back seat and choosing places to stay that work for a family without costing too much.

I have a long layover of eleven hours in Istanbul on my way to visit family. My flight lands at six in the morning and the next one leaves at five in the evening. I have heard that some travellers leave the airport and see a bit of the city. I would like to know how people usually plan a day like this, how long the transfer takes and what is realistic to see in that window.

My partner and I want to take a slow holiday this summer without flying. We live in the north of England and are thinking about taking the train to the continent and travelling for about two weeks. We like small towns, lakes and walking, and we do not mind a few long train days. We would like a rough route that is not too complicated to book and does not change trains too often.

I am going camping for the first time with a group of friends. We have booked a site with toilets and showers near a lake for three nights in early autumn. I have a borrowed tent, a sleeping bag and a camping stove. I am not sure what else I need to bring, how cold it gets at night at that time of year, or how to cook something decent on a single burner for four people.

I want to visit my aunt in Canada next spring and stay for three weeks. It will be my first long trip abroad on my own. I am a bit nervous about the long flight, getting through customs and finding my way from the airport to her town, which is two hours away by bus. I would like a simple step by step picture of what the day of travel will look like from start to finish.

Every year our office organises a team trip, and this year I have been asked to plan it. There are fourteen people, a budget of about two hundred per person, and we can go for two days. Some people like hiking and others prefer to relax. We would like somewhere within three hours by coach, with a mix of group activities and free time, and a place to eat together in the evening.

I am writing a small web app that lets people in my building share tools like ladders and drills. Each person can list an item, mark it as available and request to borrow items from others. I am using a simple server with a database and plain HTML pages. I am not sure how to model the borrowing requests in the database, or how to show who currently has each item in the list view.

At work we have a script that reads a folder of text files every night, pulls out some numbers and writes a summary to a spreadsheet. It was written years ago, has no tests and takes almost two hours to run. Nobody wants to touch it in case something stops working. I would like a plan for making it faster and safer to change, without rewriting it from scratch over a single weekend.

I am learning to code in my spare time and have finished an introductory course in Python. I can write functions, loops and simple classes, and I have built a small command line game. I am not sure what to learn next. Some people tell me to pick up web development, others say data analysis, and others say I should learn data structures first. I have about five hours a week to spend on this.

Our team keeps arguing about code reviews. Some people leave dozens of small comments about style, and others approve large changes after a quick look. Reviews sometimes sit for days and block other work. We are six developers working on one product. I would like to suggest a few simple rules for how we review code that keep quality up without slowing everyone down or causing friction.

I have a list of a few thousand customer records in a spreadsheet. Some names are duplicated with small differences in spelling, some email addresses have spaces in them, and the dates are in three different formats. I want to clean it up so we can load it into our new system. I know a little Python and can install packages, but I have never done a data cleaning job of this size before.

My personal website is a single page I wrote by hand years ago. It loads slowly on phones, the layout looks odd on small screens and I have to edit the HTML directly every time I want to add a post. I would like to move it to something easier to update, keep it cheap or free to host and still be able to change the design myself without learning a large framework or paying for a theme.

I am building a small tool that sends a reminder email to members of my running club the day before each group run. The run times are kept in a shared calendar. I want the tool to read the calendar each morning, check if there is a run the next day and send one email to the mailing list. I would like to keep it simple, cheap to run and easy for another club member to take over later.

Our app logs a lot of information, but when something goes awry in production we still struggle to find out what happened. The logs are plain text spread across three servers and searching them takes ages. We are a small team with a modest budget. I would like to understand the usual approach to collecting logs in one place and adding enough context to each entry to trace a single user request.

I am studying for a statistics module and I keep getting confused by the difference between a confidence interval and a p value. My lecture notes explain both with formulas, but I do not have a feel for what they mean. I would like a plain explanation with an everyday example, and then a couple of practice questions I can try on my own before the class test at the end of the month.

I am in my final year and have to write a dissertation of about ten thousand words. My topic is how small towns have changed since the main shops moved online. I have read around twenty sources and have a rough outline, but I keep rewriting the introduction and making no progress on the rest. The deadline is in three months and I also have two other modules running at the same time.

I have been trying to learn Spanish for a year using an app for about fifteen minutes a day. I can read simple texts and understand slow speech, but I freeze when I try to speak. I am going to Spain for a month next summer and would like to be able to hold basic conversations by then. I have about an hour a day to spend on it and a small budget for lessons or books.

My daughter is fourteen and finds maths hard. She does her homework but takes a long time and gets upset when she does not understand a topic. Her teacher says she is capable but needs to practise more. I was never strong at maths myself, so I find it hard to help her. I would like some ideas for how to support her at home without turning every evening into a fight about it.

I am going back to study as an adult after fifteen years away from education. I have enrolled in an evening course in accounting, two nights a week, while working full time. I have forgotten how to study, how to take notes and how to plan revision. I would like a simple weekly routine that fits around my job and family and gives me a fair chance of passing the exams at the end of the year.

Our reading group meets once a month and we are running short of ideas for books. We are eight people with mixed tastes. Some like crime novels, some prefer history and a couple like science writing. We try to keep books under four hundred pages so people can finish them in time. I would like a way to choose the next few books that keeps everyone interested and gives us plenty to talk about.

I have been asked to give a ten minute talk at a team meeting about a project I finished last quarter. The project was moving our customer support inbox to a new tool. It went mostly smoothly, but there were a few rough weeks in the middle. I would like to structure the talk so it is useful for the people who will run similar projects, and keep it short and honest without dwelling on blame.

I manage a team of five people. Two of them work in the office and three are remote in different time zones. Our weekly meeting is at a time that suits the office, which means one person joins very early and another very late. People have started to skip it. I would like to find a better way to keep everyone in touch without adding more meetings or leaving the remote staff out of decisions.

I started a new job three weeks ago as a project coordinator. There is a lot of information spread across shared drives, chat channels and old emails, and I keep asking the same questions. My manager is helpful but busy. I would like a simple way to organise what I am learning, keep track of who to ask about what, and show my manager by the end of my first month that I am finding my feet.

I am self employed and work from home as a graphic designer. Some weeks I have too much work and some weeks almost none. I find it hard to switch off in the evenings because my desk is in the living room. I would like ideas for planning my week, setting boundaries with clients about reply times and building a steadier flow of work over the year without taking on clients I do not enjoy.

Our office is trying to cut down on paper. At present we print contracts, invoices and meeting notes, and file them in cabinets that take up a whole wall. Most staff are comfortable with computers, but a few prefer paper and worry about losing documents. I would like a plan for moving to digital files over six months, with a clear way to name and store things so people can find them easily.

I am preparing for my yearly review at work. Over the past twelve months I led two small projects, trained a new colleague and took on extra tasks when someone left the team. Talking about my own work has never come easily to me. I would like help writing a short summary of the year that is honest, clear and specific, and a few points I can raise about my goals for the next year.

My team has a shared task board, but nobody keeps it up to date. Cards sit in the old column for weeks, and in meetings we spend the first twenty minutes working out what is actually done. We are seven people working on several small projects at once. I would like a few simple habits we could agree on so that the board reflects reality and the meetings can focus on the work itself.

I am organising a charity bake sale at my workplace next month. We have a room booked for a lunchtime, around twenty volunteers have offered to bake, and we want to raise money for a local food bank. I need to plan who brings what, how to label items for allergies, how to handle cash and card payments and how to let everyone in the building know without flooding their inboxes.

I run a small online shop selling handmade candles. Orders have doubled in the past six months, and I spend most evenings packing boxes instead of making new stock. I have thought about hiring someone part time, but I am not sure I can afford it yet. I would like to look at which tasks take the most time and whether some of them could be simplified or done in batches each week.

I have to write a short proposal asking my department for a budget to run a training day for new staff. The day would cover our main software, our safety rules and a session on how teams work together. I have never written a proposal before. I would like a simple structure for it, a sense of how much detail to include and some advice on how to present the costs clearly to the finance team.
